lesson.title: Seeing the Ions: Writing Complete Ionic Equations
lesson.summary: A complete ionic equation rewrites every dissolved strong electrolyte as its separated ions, showing what is actually present in solution instead of hiding ions inside neutral formula units.
lesson.body:
Precipitation Reactions left off with a molecular equation, Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2 KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2 KNO3(aq), written as though lead nitrate and potassium iodide exist as intact units in water. But recall from Ionic Compounds that these substances are built from cations and anions held together by electrostatic attraction, not covalent bonds, and when a soluble ionic compound dissolves in water, that attraction is overcome and the ions separate completely, moving independently through the solution. A soluble ionic compound like this is called a strong electrolyte, precisely because it dissociates fully and conducts electricity well in solution.

A complete ionic equation makes this dissociation explicit. The rule is to rewrite every aqueous strong electrolyte as its separated ions, each with its correct charge, while leaving solids, liquids, gases, and any weak electrolytes, which do not dissociate significantly, written as whole formula units. Applying that rule to the lead iodide reaction: Pb2+(aq) + 2 NO3-(aq) + 2 K+(aq) + 2 I-(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2 K+(aq) + 2 NO3-(aq). Notice that PbI2 is written as a whole formula unit on the product side, not split into ions, because it is the insoluble solid: its ions are locked into a crystal lattice, not floating freely, so it is not a dissolved electrolyte at all.

A complete ionic equation has to balance in two ways, not just one, and checking both is good practice. Atoms still have to balance: 1 lead, 2 nitrogens, 6 oxygens, 2 potassiums, and 2 iodines appear on each side. But charge has to balance too. On the left, the total charge is plus 2 from Pb2+, plus 2 times minus 1 from the nitrate ions, plus 2 times plus 1 from the potassium ions, plus 2 times minus 1 from the iodide ions, which sums to plus 2 minus 2 plus 2 minus 2, or 0. On the right, PbI2 is a neutral solid, and 2 times plus 1 from potassium plus 2 times minus 1 from nitrate also sums to 0. Both sides carry a net charge of zero, confirming the equation is balanced.

Writing out every ion like this can feel like extra work for the same chemistry, and in a sense it is, since the complete ionic equation describes exactly the same reaction as the molecular equation. Its value is that it shows you which ions are truly reacting and which ones are simply along for the ride in solution, a distinction the next chapter will make explicit.
